section.title: Love and Obey the LORD
section.sectionRationale: This chapter closes the great opening exposition of the Shema's demand for wholehearted love, applying it to the specific character of the land ahead, a place utterly dependent on rain from heaven, and introducing the blessing-and-curse ceremony that will later be enacted at Gerizim and Ebal.
section.thesis: Moses urges the new generation, who themselves witnessed the LORD's mighty acts, to love and obey Him continually, promising that a land utterly dependent on rain from heaven will flourish only under a people who fix His words in their hearts, since blessing and curse both stand ready at Gerizim and Ebal, waiting on their obedience.
section.frameNote: Six movements: remember what your own eyes have seen; a land that drinks rain from heaven; the blessing of obedience in seasonal rain; fixing these words in heart and home; every place you tread will be yours; and the blessing and curse set at Gerizim and Ebal.

units.label: Remember what your eyes have seen
units.note: your own eyes, not your children's

verses.text: You shall therefore love the LORD your God and always keep His charge, His statutes, His ordinances, and His commandments.
Know this day that it is not your children who have known and seen the discipline of the LORD your God: His greatness, His mighty hand, and His outstretched arm;
the signs and works He did in Egypt to Pharaoh king of Egypt and all his land;
what He did to the Egyptian army and horses and chariots when He made the waters of the Red Sea engulf them as they pursued you, and how He destroyed them completely, even to this day;
what He did for you in the wilderness until you reached this place;

and what He did in the midst of all the Israelites to Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab the Reubenite, when the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, their households, their tents, and every living thing that belonged to them.
For it is your own eyes that have seen every great work that the LORD has done.

units.label: A land that drinks rain from heaven

verses.text: You shall therefore keep every commandment I am giving you today, so that you may have the strength to go in and possess the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess,
and so that you may live long in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give them and their descendants, a land flowing with milk and honey.
For the land that you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated on foot, like a vegetable garden.
But the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess is a land of mountains and valleys that drinks in the rain from heaven.
It is a land for which the LORD your God cares; the eyes of the LORD your God are always on it, from the beginning to the end of the year.

units.label: The blessing of obedience: rain in season

verses.text: So if you carefully obey the commandments I am giving you today, to love the LORD your God and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul,
then I will provide rain for your land in season, the autumn and spring rains, that you may gather your grain, new wine, and oil.
And I will provide grass in the fields for your livestock, and you will eat and be satisfied.
But be careful that you are not enticed to turn aside to worship and bow down to other gods,

or the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you. He will shut the heavens so that there will be no rain, nor will the land yield its produce, and you will soon perish from the good land that the LORD is giving you.

units.label: Fix these words in your heart

verses.text: Fix these words of mine in your hearts and minds; tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads.
Teach them to your children, speaking about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.
Write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates,
so that as long as the heavens are above the earth, your days and those of your children may be multiplied in the land that the LORD swore to give your fathers.

units.label: Every place you tread will be yours

verses.text: For if you carefully keep all these commandments I am giving you to follow, to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, and to {{dabaq|hold fast}} to Him,
then the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and stronger than you.
Every place where the sole of your foot treads will be yours. Your territory will extend from the wilderness to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates River to the Western Sea.
No man will be able to stand against you; the LORD your God will put the fear and dread of you upon all the land, wherever you set foot, as He has promised you.

units.label: Blessing and curse: Gerizim and Ebal

verses.text: See, today I am setting before you a {{berakah|blessing}} and a {{qelalah|curse}},
a blessing if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God that I am giving you today,
but a curse if you disobey the commandments of the LORD your God and turn aside from the path I command you today by following other gods, which you have not known.
When the LORD your God brings you into the land you are entering to possess, you are to proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.
Are not these mountains across the Jordan, west of the road toward the sunset, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah opposite Gilgal near the Oak of Moreh?
For you are about to cross the Jordan to enter and possess the land that the LORD your God is giving you. When you take possession of it and settle in it,
be careful to follow all the statutes and ordinances that I am setting before you today.

dabaq.gloss: To cling, hold fast, stay closely attached. The same word describes a man clinging to his wife in Genesis 2:24; here it pictures covenant loyalty as an intimate, tenacious attachment to God rather than distant, occasional compliance.

berakah.gloss: Blessing, favor, well-being granted by God. Set opposite the curse, it names the flourishing life that flows from covenant obedience, not as a magic reward but as the natural fruit of a right relationship with the God who provides it.

qelalah.gloss: Curse, the opposite of blessing, a state of being cut off from the flourishing that comes from God. It names the real, covenantal consequence of turning from the LORD, not an arbitrary punishment but the natural outcome of forsaking the source of life.

basic.context: Moses closes his sweeping call to love and obey God by pointing to the very land Israel is about to enter, a place utterly dependent on rain from heaven rather than human irrigation, making obedience and dependence on God inseparable from the land's own fruitfulness.
basic.hermeneutics: This is covenant instruction addressed to a specific people entering a specific land, where blessing and curse were tied to literal agricultural outcomes, rain or drought. Its enduring principle, that genuine flourishing flows from wholehearted devotion to God, carries forward even though its precise agricultural form belonged to Israel's particular covenant.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel is called to dabaq, cling or hold fast, to the LORD, the same intimate word used of marriage in Genesis 2:24. Moses sets before them berakah, blessing, and qelalah, curse, real covenantal outcomes flowing naturally from faithfulness or unfaithfulness to the God who alone gives the land its rain.
basic.typology: The choice of blessing or curse set before Israel at Gerizim and Ebal anticipates the ultimate choice of life or death, blessing or curse, that the gospel presents to every person, resolved fully in Christ, who was made a curse for His people so they might receive the blessing, Galatians 3:13-14.
basic.christ: Paul draws directly on Deuteronomy's blessing-and-curse language in Galatians 3:13-14, explaining that Christ redeemed His people from the law's curse by becoming a curse for them, so that the blessing promised to Abraham might come to all who trust in Him.
basic.god: God cares personally for the land itself, His eyes upon it continually from the beginning of the year to its end, and He ties Israel's flourishing directly to their wholehearted devotion, showing that His blessings are not arbitrary but flow from a real, dependent relationship with Him.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 27:11-13 and Joshua 8:30-35 record the later, literal enactment of the blessing and curse ceremony on Gerizim and Ebal. Galatians 3:13-14 identifies Christ as the one who bears the covenant curse so believers receive the blessing. Ephesians 6:1-3 echoes the pattern of teaching children continually.
basic.oneStory: This chapter presents obedience and dependence on God as inseparable from real, tangible flourishing, setting a stark choice of blessing or curse before God's people. That choice reaches its climactic resolution in Christ, who bears the curse Himself so that every person who trusts Him receives the blessing instead.

context.literary:
Chapter 11 is the closing appeal of the long sermon that began in chapter 5, and it deliberately gathers up what came before. Verse 1 restates the command to love the LORD, verses 18 to 20 repeat almost word for word the instructions of 6:6-9 about hands, foreheads, children and doorposts, and verse 23 echoes the 'nations greater and stronger than you' of 9:1. The repetition works like the final movement of a symphony returning to its opening themes.

The chapter moves in a clear sequence. Verses 2 to 7 look back: what your own eyes have seen. Verses 8 to 17 look at the land itself, contrasting Egypt and Canaan, and set out the two ways the rain might go. Verses 18 to 21 turn to the home and the next generation. Verses 22 to 25 look outward to the borders of the land. Verses 26 to 32 then bring everything to a point of decision, a blessing and a curse set before Israel, to be proclaimed on two mountains.

That last paragraph is also a hinge in the book. Its call to 'follow all the statutes and ordinances,' verse 32, is picked up directly by 12:1, 'These are the statutes and ordinances,' and the detailed laws of chapters 12 to 26 follow. The ceremony at Gerizim and Ebal is promised here and then described after those laws in chapter 27. The law code is therefore framed by blessing and curse, with chapters 11 and 27 standing like two mountains on either side of it.

The chapter also shifts between singular and plural address, as Deuteronomy often does. Verse 26 begins with a singular 'See' and continues with a plural 'before you.' Moses speaks to the nation as one person and to its members as many, since the choice is both corporate and individual.
context.historical:
The contrast of verses 10 to 12 would have been obvious to people who grew up in Egypt. Egyptian farming depended on the Nile's annual flood and on channels that carried its water to the fields. Watering 'on foot' probably refers to that labor, whether working a water-lifting device with the feet or opening and closing small earth channels by kicking them. Either way, water in Egypt came up from below and was managed by human effort. Canaan's hill country had no great river. Its farming depended on rain, and on its timing: the early rains that softened the ground for ploughing and sowing in autumn, and the late rains of spring that filled out the grain before harvest.

This made rain a religious question. The Canaanites credited their storm god Baal with sending it, which is why Israel was constantly tempted to 'turn aside' to other gods, verse 16. Hosea later complains that Israel did not acknowledge 'that it was I who gave her grain, new wine, and oil,' Hosea 2:8, using the same triad as verse 14. The drought of Elijah's day, 1 Kings 17:1, was a direct challenge to Baal on his own ground, answered when the LORD sent rain after the contest on Carmel, 1 Kings 18:41-45.

The judgment on Dathan and Abiram, verse 6, is described in Numbers 16. Moses names these two Reubenites and does not mention Korah, as Psalm 106:17 also names only Dathan and Abiram. Numbers 26:11 notes that 'the line of Korah did not die out,' and the whole households of the two Reubenites were swallowed, which may be why they are singled out here.

Gerizim and Ebal stand on either side of the pass at Shechem, in the heart of the land. It was at 'the Oak of Moreh at Shechem' that God first promised the land to Abram and Abram built an altar, Genesis 12:6-7. Moses sends Israel back to the very place where the promise began. Joshua carried out the ceremony there, Joshua 8:30-35, and later renewed the covenant at Shechem, Joshua 24:1. The borders of verse 24, from the wilderness to Lebanon and from the Euphrates to the Mediterranean, echo the promise of Genesis 15:18 and were approached in Solomon's reign, 1 Kings 4:21.
context.canonical:
The rain promises of this chapter shape the rest of Israel's story. Leviticus 26:4 and Deuteronomy 28:12 make rain in season a covenant blessing, and Deuteronomy 28:23-24 makes bronze skies and dust for rain a covenant curse. Solomon's dedication prayer asks God to forgive and send rain 'when the skies are shut' because of sin, 1 Kings 8:35-36, using the language of verse 17, and God answers in 2 Chronicles 7:13-14. Jeremiah laments that Judah never said, 'Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rains, both autumn and spring,' Jeremiah 5:24. Joel promises the return of those same rains, Joel 2:23, and Zechariah 14:17 still speaks of rain withheld from those who will not worship the King.

The instructions of verses 18 to 21 became part of the daily life of Judaism. Together with 6:4-9, verses 13 to 21 form the second paragraph of the Shema recited morning and evening, and both passages are written on the parchments placed in the mezuzah on the doorpost and in the phylacteries. Jesus criticized those who 'broaden their phylacteries' for show, Matthew 23:5, not the practice of binding God's word itself.

The blessing and curse of verses 26 to 29 are developed in chapters 27 and 28 and come to their climax in Moses' final call, 'I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life,' Deuteronomy 30:19. Psalm 1 turns that choice into a portrait of two ways. In the New Testament Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at the foot of Gerizim, the mountain of blessing, where her people worshiped, John 4:20. Paul explains that 'all who rely on works of the law are under a curse,' Galatians 3:10, and that Christ redeemed us from it by becoming a curse, so that the blessing of Abraham reaches the Gentiles, Galatians 3:13-14. James draws on the early and late rains to teach patience, James 5:7, and on Elijah's prayer for rain, James 5:17-18.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses is addressing people who had personally witnessed God's acts, and he insists on it: 'it is not your children who have known and seen,' verse 2, but 'your own eyes,' verse 7. Their experience carries responsibility. They cannot plead ignorance, and they must become the witnesses who tell the next generation.

His deeper aim is to make Israel understand the land as a school of dependence. In Egypt water was a matter of engineering. In Canaan it would be a matter of prayer and faithfulness, for the land lived under the eye of God from one end of the year to the other. Every season of rain or drought would be a reminder of whom they served. Moses wants them to feel that devotion to the LORD is not a religious compartment but the condition of their bread.

Finally, he wants to bring them to a decision. The chapter ends not with information but with a choice set before them 'today,' to be ratified in the land itself on two mountains, so that the whole nation would take on the covenant with their own voices.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The specific link between obedience and rainfall belongs to the national covenant God made with Israel in Canaan. Scripture itself shows it is not a mechanical rule for every person: Jesus says the Father 'sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous,' Matthew 5:45, and Job's story warns against reading suffering as proof of sin. Nor does the chapter command believers to perform a ceremony on Gerizim and Ebal, or promise the church territory from the Euphrates to the sea.

What carries over is substantial. The call to love God, to walk in His ways and to hold fast to Him is repeated in the New Testament. The command to saturate home life with God's word, in conversation, at rising and lying down, remains a pattern for Christian households, Ephesians 6:4 and Colossians 3:16. The warning that the heart can be quietly enticed to other gods applies to every idol that promises provision. And the choice between blessing and curse is still set before every hearer, now resolved in Christ who bore the curse, Galatians 3:13.

debates.question: Does the rain-blessing and drought-curse pattern in this chapter apply directly to believers' material circumstances today?

views.label: This is a specific covenant sign tied to Israel's land, not a universal formula
views.case: The blessing and curse here are covenant sanctions specific to Israel's unique national relationship with God in a particular land; the New Testament does not promise believers material prosperity in exchange for obedience, and many faithful believers suffer hardship, 2 Corinthians 11:23-28.

views.label: It illustrates a broader, ongoing principle of dependence on God
views.case: While the specific agricultural sign was unique to Israel, the underlying principle, that turning from God leads to spiritual barrenness and turning to Him leads to flourishing, however defined, remains a real pattern in the Christian life, even if its outworking is not primarily material.

debates.bearing: Both views agree this passage should not be used to promise material wealth in exchange for obedience today, while affirming that genuine spiritual flourishing does flow from wholehearted devotion to God.

debates.question: Are the commands to tie God's words on hands and foreheads and write them on doorposts, verses 18 to 20, meant literally or figuratively?

views.label: Literal commands to be carried out
views.case: Jewish practice has long read these verses literally, placing the texts in phylacteries and in the mezuzah on the doorpost. The instructions are concrete, and Deuteronomy 27:2-3 does command words of the law to be physically written on stones. Jesus criticized only the enlarging of phylacteries for display, Matthew 23:5, not their use.

views.label: Vivid figures for constant, visible devotion
views.case: Others note that Proverbs uses the same images figuratively, 'bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart,' Proverbs 3:3 and 7:3, and that verse 18 begins with the heart. On this reading the hands stand for action, the forehead for thought, and the doorposts and gates for home and public life.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the point is that God's word should shape every sphere of life, private and public. Whether or not a physical reminder is used, it is worthless if the words are not first fixed in the heart, which is where verse 18 begins.

debates.question: Does the conditional 'if you carefully obey' of verses 13 and 22 contradict chapter 9's insistence that Israel does not receive the land because of its righteousness?

views.label: Grace gives the land; obedience is the way of living in it
views.case: Chapter 9 concerns why Israel receives the land at all, and the answer is God's oath. Chapter 11 concerns how Israel will flourish and remain in it. The conditions are not a price paid for the gift but the shape of life within the relationship, as in Exodus 15:26, which promises blessing to the people God had already redeemed.

views.label: The conditions expose Israel's need
views.case: Others stress that Deuteronomy expects Israel to fail the conditions, 31:16-21, and that the curse of drought and exile will come. On this reading the conditional promises function, as Paul argues in Galatians 3:10, to show that blessing cannot finally rest on the people's performance and must come through another.

debates.bearing: The two readings work together. The land is a gift of grace, and obedience is the fitting response within it, yet Israel's actual history shows that the heart able to keep the conditions must itself be given, Deuteronomy 30:6.

study.originalLanguages:
In verse 2 Israel is told to know 'the discipline of the LORD,' using musar. The word means instruction that corrects, the training a father gives a son, and it is the word of Proverbs 3:11, 'do not reject the discipline of the LORD,' quoted in Hebrews 12:5. Deuteronomy 8:5 uses its verb: 'as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you.' So the plagues on Egypt, the Red Sea, the wilderness and the judgment on Dathan and Abiram are all presented as education. God's mighty acts were lessons in who He is.

Verse 12 says the land is one 'for which the LORD your God cares.' The verb is darash, which usually means to seek, inquire or look after. The land is sought out by God, attended to, and 'the eyes of the LORD your God are always on it, from the beginning to the end of the year.' 'Beginning' is reshit and 'end' is acharit, a pair that spans the whole agricultural cycle. The same verb darash appears in Micah 6:8 for what the LORD 'requires.' Israel's land is under constant, personal attention.

The rains of verse 14 are named with two technical terms: yoreh, the early or autumn rain, and malqosh, the late or spring rain. They appear together again in Jeremiah 5:24 and Joel 2:23, and James 5:7 carries the pair into Greek when he speaks of the farmer waiting 'for the fall and spring rains.' The produce named in the same verse, grain, new wine and oil, dagan, tirosh and yitshar, is the standard triad of Israel's harvest. The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew has 'I will provide,' with God speaking in the first person through Moses, while the Samaritan Pentateuch and Septuagint read 'He will provide.'

The warning of verse 16, 'be careful that you are not enticed,' is literally 'lest your heart be enticed,' from patah, to be open, simple or easily persuaded. The same verb describes a heart 'secretly enticed' to worship the sun and moon in Job 31:27. Idolatry here is not pictured as a bold rebellion but as a naive heart talked into it. The curse of verse 17, 'He will shut the heavens,' uses atsar, to restrain or close up, the verb that returns in Solomon's prayer 'when the skies are shut,' 1 Kings 8:35.

Verse 18 literally says 'you shall place these words of mine on your heart and on your soul,' levav and nephesh, which the BSB renders 'hearts and minds.' The words are to be set upon the inner person before they are bound on the hand. The promise of verse 21, 'as long as the heavens are above the earth,' is literally 'like the days of the heavens over the earth,' an idiom for permanence, which Psalm 89:29 echoes when it promises David's throne will last 'as long as the heavens endure.'

Finally, 'See,' in verse 26, is the imperative re'eh, singular, addressed to Israel as one, while 'before you' is plural. The Jewish lectionary names the reading that begins here after this word. The choice is set before each Israelite and before the nation together.

typology.type: The blessing and curse set at Gerizim and Ebal
typology.fulfillment: Israel was to hear the blessing from one mountain and the curse from the other, and Paul shows that the curse was not a distant possibility: 'All who rely on works of the law are under a curse,' Galatians 3:10. In Christ the two mountains meet on one hill. He 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13, quoting Deuteronomy 21:23, so that 'the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles,' Galatians 3:14. The type falls short in that Israel's ceremony only announced blessing and curse; Christ absorbs the one and gives the other. Revelation 22:3 records the end: 'No longer will there be any curse.'

typology.type: A land that drinks rain from heaven, not human irrigation
typology.fulfillment: Canaan could not be watered by effort from below; it waited for rain from above. Scripture uses the same image for the Spirit. God promises, 'I will pour water on the thirsty land... I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants,' Isaiah 44:3. Jesus offers living water to the Samaritan woman near Gerizim, John 4:10-14, and at the feast He promises streams of living water, 'speaking about the Spirit,' John 7:37-39. The escalation is that the rain no longer falls on a territory but within people. Where rain could be withheld from a disobedient land, the Spirit is given as the gift of Christ's finished work.

typology.type: Every place the sole of your foot treads, from the wilderness to the Euphrates
typology.fulfillment: The promise of verse 24 was only partly realized in Israel's history, approached under Solomon, 1 Kings 4:21, and lost in exile. The New Testament widens it. Paul calls the promise to Abraham a promise that he would be 'heir of the world,' Romans 4:13, and Jesus says the meek 'will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5. Abraham himself looked beyond the land to 'the city with foundations,' Hebrews 11:10. The type falls short because its borders could be crossed and its tenure lost; the inheritance in Christ is the whole renewed creation, and it cannot be taken away.

study.christ:
The chapter's pattern of love, obedience, remembered words and the land's fruitfulness leads to Christ in several ways, and the New Testament names them.

First, Christ is the true Israelite in whom verse 18 is fulfilled. God's words were fixed in His heart. He answered every temptation with Deuteronomy and said His food was to do the will of the One who sent Him. Where Israel's heart was 'enticed' to other gods, verse 16, His was undivided. Jesus also defines blessing in the chapter's own terms, 'Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it,' Luke 11:28, and He links love and obedience exactly as Moses does: 'If you love Me, you will keep My commandments,' John 14:15.

Second, Christ resolves the choice of verses 26 to 28. The ceremony at Gerizim and Ebal set two outcomes before a people who, as Deuteronomy itself foresees, would choose badly. Paul reads the curse as the verdict hanging over all who rely on the law, Galatians 3:10, and announces that Christ became that curse, hanging on a tree, Galatians 3:13 and Deuteronomy 21:23. The blessing that was pronounced from Gerizim was thereby opened to the nations, Galatians 3:14. It is fitting that John records Jesus sitting at Jacob's well in the shadow of Gerizim, offering 'the gift of God' to a Samaritan woman, John 4:5-10, and telling her that the hour was coming when worship would not be tied to that mountain or to Jerusalem.

Third, the rain. Moses tells Israel that the land lives from heaven's gift. The prophets turn that into a picture of God's own coming: 'He will come to us like the rain,' Hosea 6:3, and of the Spirit poured out like water on dry ground, Isaiah 44:3. Jesus fulfils both. He is the One from heaven, and He gives the Spirit as living water, John 7:37-39. Believers are like the land of verse 11, unable to water themselves; apart from Him they can do nothing, John 15:5.

Fourth, the discipline of verse 2. The Lord's discipline of Israel in the wilderness is applied by Hebrews to the church as the loving training of sons, Hebrews 12:5-11. Jesus Himself, though a Son, 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8, and the Father disciplines those united to Him 'for our good, so that we may share in His holiness,' Hebrews 12:10.

A caution belongs here. The New Testament does not treat every detail of the chapter as a picture of Christ, and there is no warrant to find Him in the doorposts or the phylacteries. The links run through the chapter's main lines: the word in the heart, the blessing and curse, the gift from heaven.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He acts in history and wants those acts remembered. Verses 2 to 7 list His works: signs in Egypt, the sea closing over the army, provision in the wilderness, judgment on Dathan and Abiram. These are called His 'discipline,' verse 2. God is a teacher who instructs His people through events, and the memory of those events is meant to produce love and obedience in those who saw them.

Second, God is the giver of rain. Verse 14 even puts it in His own voice, 'I will provide rain.' Rain in Canaan was not an impersonal force of nature or the gift of a storm god; it came from the hand of the LORD, as Paul told the crowd at Lystra, 'He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons,' Acts 14:17. Scripture holds together God's general kindness, rain on the just and unjust, Matthew 5:45, and His covenant dealings with Israel, where rain became a sign of His favor or displeasure.

Third, God's care is personal and constant. The land is one He 'seeks,' and His eyes are 'always on it, from the beginning to the end of the year,' verse 12. God is not a distant proprietor but an attentive owner. The image anticipates the psalmist's confidence that the Lord attends to the earth and waters it, Psalm 65:9-10. His providence reaches to every season and every field.

Fourth, God is jealous for undivided devotion. The anger of verse 17 is kindled not by weakness but by turning aside 'to worship and bow down to other gods.' The same God who loves His people will withhold rain rather than let them believe it comes from Baal. His judgments serve His love: He would rather His people be thirsty and turn back than be satisfied and lost.

Fifth, God is faithful to His oath. Verses 9 and 21 speak of 'the land that the LORD swore to your fathers,' and verse 25 adds 'as He has promised you.' The borders He sets, the dread He puts on the nations, and the days He multiplies all flow from promises already made. The blessing and curse are not arbitrary; they are the outworking of His covenant word.

For worship, this means gratitude for ordinary gifts. Every meal and every harvest is to be received as from His hand. It also means seriousness, since the God who gives can withhold. And it means hope, because the God whose eyes are on the land from the year's beginning to its end is the God who keeps His people from beginning to end.

crossReferences.note: The first statement of the instructions repeated in 11:18-20: words upon the heart, taught to children, spoken of at home and on the road, tied on hands and foreheads, written on doorposts. Moses closes the sermon by returning to the Shema, framing chapters 6 to 11 as one sustained call to love God.

The detailed instructions for the ceremony promised in 11:29, naming the six tribes who stand on Gerizim to bless and the six who stand on Ebal for the curse. The two passages bracket the law code of chapters 12 to 26.

Joshua builds an altar on Ebal, writes a copy of the law on stones, and reads 'all the words of the law, the blessings and the curses' with half of Israel before each mountain, foreigners included. Moses' command of Deuteronomy 11:29 was carried out once the people entered the land.

At the Oak of Moreh near Shechem God first promised the land to Abram's offspring, and Abram built an altar. Deuteronomy 11:30 locates Gerizim and Ebal by the same landmark, sending Israel to ratify the covenant at the spot where the promise was first spoken.

Solomon asks God to hear and forgive 'when the skies are shut and there is no rain because Your people have sinned.' He treats the curse of Deuteronomy 11:17 as a real possibility and turns it into a call for confession and prayer toward God's house.

God complains that Israel did not acknowledge 'that it was I who gave her grain, new wine, and oil,' crediting Baal instead. The prophet names the exact triad of Deuteronomy 11:14 and shows the enticement of 11:16 fulfilled in Israel's history.

Moses' final form of the choice first set out in 11:26: 'I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life.' The blessing and curse of chapter 11 are revealed to be matters of life and death.

Paul quotes Deuteronomy's curse on everyone who does not keep the law and announces that Christ became a curse, hanging on a tree, so that Abraham's blessing reaches the Gentiles. The choice of Gerizim and Ebal is resolved by a substitute who takes the curse himself.

At the foot of Gerizim the Samaritan woman says, 'Our fathers worshiped on this mountain.' Jesus answers that true worship will be in spirit and truth. The mountain of blessing from Deuteronomy 11:29 becomes the setting for the announcement that blessing is now found in the Messiah Himself.

Hebrews quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 on the Lord's discipline and applies it to believers as sons. The musar of Deuteronomy 11:2, God's training of Israel through His acts, becomes the Father's loving discipline of the church, 'so that we may share in His holiness.'

James tells believers to wait for the Lord's coming as the farmer waits 'for the fall and spring rains,' the pair named in Deuteronomy 11:14. The dependence the land taught Israel becomes a lesson in patient hope for the church.

The psalmist resolves to tell the next generation the LORD's works, as God commanded the fathers to teach their children, so that they would 'put their confidence in God.' It is a living example of Deuteronomy 11:19, teaching passed from parents who saw to children who did not.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a garden watered by God, where 'the LORD God had not yet sent rain upon the earth' until He planted and provided, Genesis 2:5-6. Humanity lived from His hand. After the fall the ground was cursed, Genesis 3:17-18, and bread came by toil. Deuteronomy 11 stands between those two worlds. Canaan is not Eden, but it is a land that must be watered from heaven, a place where Israel would learn again to live by God's gift rather than by the effort of the foot.

The chapter answers the exodus. The God who struck Egypt and split the sea has made Himself known, and the generation who saw it is charged to love Him and to pass on the memory. It also sets up everything that follows. The blessing and curse announced here are pronounced on Gerizim and Ebal in Joshua 8, and the history of Israel in the land becomes the story of those two words. The skies were shut in Elijah's day. The curse finally fell in exile, and the land that drank the rain of heaven lay desolate.

The prophets looked past that curse to a new outpouring. God promised to send 'showers of blessing,' Ezekiel 34:26, to pour water on the thirsty land and His Spirit on Israel's offspring, Isaiah 44:3. The rain became a picture of the Spirit, and the land a picture of the human heart.

In Christ the story turns. He bears the curse announced from Ebal, Galatians 3:13, and pours out the Spirit promised like rain, John 7:39. The blessing of Abraham reaches the nations. Those who were never part of Israel's tribes come to stand on the mountain of blessing through faith in Him.

The story ends in a new creation where the river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life yields fruit every month, Revelation 22:1-2. There will be no drought and no need to watch the sky. 'No longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3. The land that God cared for from the beginning of the year to its end becomes the whole earth under His eye forever.

quiz.q: How does Moses contrast the land of Canaan with the land of Egypt (vv.10-11)?

options.text: Egypt required manual irrigation like a garden, but Canaan drinks rain from heaven, directly dependent on the LORD's care.
options.note: Verses 10-11 make exactly this contrast.

options.text: Egypt was barren while Canaan required irrigation.
options.note: The text reverses this: Egypt required irrigation, and Canaan depends on rainfall.

options.text: Both lands required identical farming methods.
options.note: The whole point of these verses is to highlight a sharp contrast, not a similarity.

options.text: No comparison between the two lands is made.
options.note: Verses 10-11 make an explicit, detailed comparison.

quiz.q: What promise is tied to obedience regarding rainfall (vv.13-14)?

options.text: The LORD would provide autumn and spring rains in season so Israel could gather grain, wine, and oil.
options.note: Verses 13-14 state this promise directly.

options.text: Rain would fall constantly regardless of obedience.
options.note: The promise is conditioned explicitly on obedience, not unconditional constancy.

options.text: Israel would never need rain again.
options.note: The chapter's whole point is Israel's ongoing need for and dependence on rain.

options.text: No connection between obedience and rain is made.
options.note: Verses 13-17 draw this connection explicitly, both positively and negatively.

quiz.q: What are Israelites told to do with God's words according to verses 18-20?

options.text: Fix them in heart and mind, teach them to children, and write them on doorposts and gates.
options.note: Verses 18-20 give this exact instruction.

options.text: Bury them in a sealed container.
options.note: No such instruction appears; the words are to be actively kept visible and taught, not buried.

options.text: Recite them only once a year at a single festival.
options.note: The instruction describes continual, daily teaching, not an annual recitation.

options.text: Nothing is instructed regarding God's words in this passage.
options.note: Verses 18-20 give explicit, detailed instructions.

quiz.q: What two mountains are named for pronouncing blessing and curse (v.29)?

options.text: The blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.
options.note: Verse 29 names these two mountains specifically.

options.text: Mount Sinai and Mount Horeb.
options.note: These are the mountains associated with the giving of the law, not this blessing-and-curse ceremony.

options.text: Mount Nebo and Mount Pisgah.
options.note: These mountains are associated with Moses viewing the land, not this ceremony.

options.text: No mountains are mentioned.
options.note: Verse 29 names two specific mountains.

quiz.q: What two things does Moses say he is setting before Israel today (v.26)?

options.text: A blessing and a curse.
options.note: Verse 26 states this explicitly.

options.text: Two different laws to choose between.
options.note: The choice is between obedience and disobedience to the one law, framed as blessing versus curse, not between two separate laws.

options.text: Two kings to choose between.
options.note: No kingship choice is presented in this verse.

options.text: Nothing is set before Israel in this verse.
options.note: Verse 26 makes an explicit statement.

questions: Unlike Egypt's self-sufficient irrigation, Canaan's fruitfulness depended entirely on rain from heaven, a picture of ongoing dependence on God. Where in your life have you built a self-sufficient system that quietly reduces your need to depend on Him?
Moses calls Israel to fix God's words in their hearts and minds continually, not occasionally. What practical rhythms actually keep God's word fixed in your heart day to day?
Blessing and curse stood before Israel as a real choice with real consequences. What choice are you facing right now where the stakes of obedience or disobedience feel unusually clear?

Moses reminds the people that their own eyes saw the LORD's discipline and deliverance, urging active remembering rather than secondhand hearing. What has God done in your own life that you need to remember more deliberately?

The command to teach children 'when you sit at home and when you walk along the road' pictures faith woven into ordinary movement, not confined to formal settings. Where does faith show up naturally in your daily routine, and where is it conspicuously missing?

translationNotes.note: 'Irrigated on foot' likely describes ancient Egyptian methods of using foot-powered devices or channels to move Nile water to fields, a labor-intensive, human-controlled process contrasted sharply with rain-dependent Canaan.
'Every place where the sole of your foot treads' is an idiom for extensive territorial promise, echoed again when God commissions Joshua in Joshua 1:3.
This blessing-and-curse ceremony anticipated here is given fuller instruction in Deuteronomy 27 and literally carried out in Joshua 8:30-35 after Israel enters the land.
